question: While the European Union has been adopting one regulation or directive after another in the field of biodiversity, many bird species are in critical danger of extinction due to the Commission’s globalist and ultra-liberal ideology.

The numerous free trade agreements have considerably intensified maritime traffic, leading to an increase in spills of chemicals, hydrocarbons and other polluting substances and, consequently, disrupting the wintering of birds. This phenomenon alters food resources, hinders the migratory behaviour of birds and is causing a worrying decline in bird populations in Europe.

At the same time, rapid urbanisation in the form unregulated urban sprawl is mercilessly devouring natural areas. This industrial, residential and commercial expansion is pushing animal species out of their habitats, leaving them with just small pockets of land and depriving them of vital resources. 1.
What action does the Commission intend to take to reduce maritime pollution caused by the numerous free trade agreements?
What mechanisms does it have at its disposal to encourage Member States to reduce urban sprawl?
How does the Commission intend to halt the decline in bird populations on our continent?
answer: 1. The EU Biodiversity Strategy for 2030 (1) committed to ensure full implementation and enforcement of the biodiversity provisions in all trade agreements on biodiversity and to better assess the impact of trade agreements on biodiversity, with follow-up action to strengthen biodiversity provisions of existing and new agreements if relevant (2).

The Commission published a methodology to assess trade liberalisation impacts on biodiversity (3). This methodology will help to identify actions to strengthen the biodiversity provisions of trade agreements. The Commission is also carrying out an ex-post evaluation of the impact of trade agreements on key environmental aspects (4). 2.

In accordance with the EU Soil Strategy for 2030 (5), the Commission will develop guidance to public authorities and private companies on how to reduce soil sealing with a revision of the EU Soil Sealing Guidelines (6) by 2024. 3. The Birds Directive (7) aims to protect all naturally occurring wild bird species present in the EU and their most important habitats.

To achieve these aims, EU Member States are required to take measures concerning the protection and restoration of the birds’ habitats (8), as well as to establish a general system of protection of birds and to ensure that the taking of birds is sustainable.

The draft Nature Restoration Law (9), currently under provisional interinstitutional agreement, builds on the Birds Directive and requires Member States to put in place restoration measures to improve the quality and quantity of the habitats of bird species and to increase the common bird indexes. The Commission is supporting Member States in their efforts to implement the above-mentioned provisions.
